x: Sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) is called the King of Chemicals because it is used in so many industries, from fertilisers to batteries.
t: Recall the common titles of acids.

x: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂, is Milk of Magnesia, a mild base that neutralises excess stomach acid. NaOH and KOH are too strong to swallow.
t: Recall the common names of bases.

x: Gypsum heated at 373 K (100°C) loses some water to give Plaster of Paris, CaSO₄·½H₂O. Overheating gives dead-burnt plaster.
t: Recall 373 K for Plaster of Paris.

x: Option C is incorrect: magnesium sulphate is Epsom salt, while bleaching powder is calcium oxychloride. The other common names are right.
t: Recall the common name of each salt.

x: Both are true and R explains A: an acid and a base reacting to give salt and water, releasing heat, is what neutralisation means.
t: Check whether R defines A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: carbonic acid forms because CO₂ dissolves in water; its presence in soda and rain is only where it occurs.
t: Check whether R is a cause or only an occurrence.

x: Statement A is true: phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base. Statement B is false because it reverses methyl orange, which is red in acid and yellow in base.
t: Recall indicator colours in acid and base.

x: HCl is muriatic acid, HNO₃ aqua fortis, H₂SO₄ oil of vitriol and CH₃COOH is vinegar, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the old names of acids.

x: Bleaching powder disinfects, Plaster of Paris makes casts, copper sulphate is a fungicide and washing soda softens water, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the uses of common salts.

x: I and II are correct: NaOH and KOH are bases, and NaCl and NaHCO₃ are salts. III is false because non-metal oxides such as CO₂ and SO₂ are acidic.
t: Discriminate metal oxides (basic) from non-metal oxides (acidic).

x: All four are correct: citric acid in citrus fruits, lactic acid in curd, formic acid in ant and bee stings and malic acid in apples.
t: Recall the natural source of each acid.

x: Both are true and R explains A: HCl is secreted in gastric juice because it is needed to activate digestion in the stomach.
t: Check whether R is the reason for A.

x: Citric acid C₆H₈O₇ is in lemons, tartaric acid C₄H₆O₆ in tamarind, oxalic acid C₂H₂O₄ in tomatoes and spinach, and formic acid HCOOH in nettle, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the formula and source of each acid.

x: All three are correct: lactic acid is C₃H₆O₃ and builds up in muscles after exercise, and malic acid is C₄H₆O₅.
t: Recall the formulas of natural acids.

x: Both are true: ascorbic acid is vitamin C and is found in amla, guava and citrus fruits.
t: Recall the source of vitamin C.

x: Both are true: carbonic acid is H₂CO₃ and phosphoric acid is H₃PO₄.
t: Recall the formulas of common acids.

x: Phosphoric acid is used in soft drinks, sulphuric acid in batteries, nitric acid in explosives and HCl in cleaning metals, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the use of each acid.

x: HCl is used in digestion, metal cleaning, pickling and dyes. Since every List-II entry is HCl, the code pairs them in order, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that the code pairs items in order when List-II repeats.

x: Both are true: acetic acid is the acid in vinegar and is widely used as a food preservative.
t: Recall the uses of acetic acid.

x: All six are correct: citric and tartaric acids are both used in food, soft drinks and medicines.
t: Recall the uses of fruit acids.

x: Oxalic acid removes ink and rust stains because it binds iron. Acetic, citric and tartaric acids are mainly food acids.
t: Recall the use of each acid.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: ascorbic acid as vitamin C has nothing to do with phosphoric acid in detergents.
t: Check whether R is related to A.

x: All four are correct: NaOH is caustic soda, a strong corrosive base used for soap, paper, rayon and degreasing.
t: Recall the properties and uses of NaOH.

x: KOH is caustic potash, a strong base used in soap and batteries, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate caustic potash (KOH) from caustic soda (NaOH).

x: Option D is incorrect: slaked lime is used for whitewash, bleaching powder and soil neutralisation, while water softening uses washing soda. The other facts are right.
t: Recall the uses of slaked lime.

x: Both are true: magnesium hydroxide is a mild base, and ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH) is a weak base used in cleaners.
t: Recall the strength of common bases.

x: All three are correct: calcium oxide, CaO, is quicklime and is used in cement.
t: Discriminate quicklime (CaO) from slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂).

x: Option A is incorrect: sodium carbonate (washing soda) comes from a strong base and a weak acid, so it is a basic salt.
t: Recall that strong base plus weak acid gives a basic salt.

x: Sodium chloride is NaCl, called common salt, obtained from sea water and rock salt, and formed from HCl + NaOH, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the facts about common salt.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the chlor-alkali process is an industrial use, not why salt is used in food.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a parallel use.

x: All five are correct: NaHCO₃ is made by the Solvay process from NaCl and used in baking, as an antacid and in fire extinguishers.
t: Recall the uses of baking soda.

x: Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, made by recrystallising sodium carbonate and used for cleaning and glass, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the facts about washing soda.

x: Bleaching powder is CaOCl₂, made from Ca(OH)₂ and Cl₂, Plaster of Paris is CaSO₄·½H₂O and blue vitriol is CuSO₄·5H₂O, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the formulas of common salts.

x: Both are true: Epsom salt is MgSO₄·7H₂O and is used in bath salts and as a laxative.
t: Recall the formula and uses of Epsom salt.

x: All three are correct: CaCO₃ occurs as limestone, marble and chalk and is used in cement, antacids and toothpaste.
t: Recall the forms and uses of calcium carbonate.

x: All five are acids: hydrochloric, sulphuric and nitric are mineral acids, while acetic and citric are organic acids.
t: Discriminate mineral from organic acids.

x: Sodium oxide and calcium oxide are basic metal oxides, Plaster of Paris is a salt and carbonic acid is acidic, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Classify each compound as acid, base, salt or oxide.

x: Both are given as true: pure water has pH 7 and is neutral, and milk is listed as about pH 7, though it is really slightly acidic, around 6.5.
t: Recall the pH of common substances.

x: All four are correct: blood is slightly basic at pH about 7.4, and baking soda solution is weakly basic at pH 8–9.
t: Recall the pH of common substances.

x: Milk of Magnesia has a pH of about 10, mildly basic. 8–9 is baking soda and 11–14 is NaOH or soap.
t: Recall the pH of common bases.

x: Blue litmus turns red in acid, red litmus turns blue in base, turmeric goes reddish-brown in base, and red cabbage is red in acid, green in base and purple when neutral, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the colour changes of indicators.

x: All four are correct: litmus has no separate neutral colour, phenolphthalein stays colourless in neutral solution and methyl orange is orange.
t: Recall the neutral colours of indicators.

x: Zinc and HCl give salt and hydrogen, acids and carbonates give salt, water and CO₂ (as in HCl + CaCO₃), and HCl + NaOH gives NaCl and water, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the products of each acid reaction.

x: HCl + CuO gives CuCl₂ + H₂O and NaOH + CO₂ gives Na₂CO₃ + H₂O, each producing salt and water. With List-II repeating, the code pairs in order, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall that oxides react with acids or bases to give salt and water.

x: Calcium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide are bases, while sodium carbonate and bleaching powder are salts, giving a-i, b-i, c-ii, d-ii.
t: Classify each compound as base or salt.

x: Both are true: gastric juice and battery acid are both strongly acidic at about pH 1–2.
t: Recall the pH of strong acids.

x: All four are correct: lemon juice and vinegar are both acidic, at about pH 2–3.
t: Recall the pH of common acids.

x: Both are true: tomato and coffee are both weakly acidic, at about pH 4–5.
t: Recall the pH of weak acids.

x: All five are correct: Milk of Magnesia is basic, and soap and NaOH solution are strongly basic at pH 11–14.
t: Recall the pH of common bases.

x: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is C₆H₈O₆. C₆H₈O₇ is citric acid, C₄H₆O₆ tartaric acid and C₃H₆O₃ lactic acid.
t: Discriminate ascorbic (O₆) from citric (O₇) acid.

x: Magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)₂. Ca(OH)₂ is slaked lime, NaOH caustic soda and NH₄OH ammonium hydroxide.
t: Recall the formulas of common bases.

x: Option C is incorrect: NaHCO₃ is baking soda, while washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. Its uses and formula are stated correctly.
t: Discriminate baking soda from washing soda.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the formula identifies the compound, while the name comes from gypsum quarried near Paris.
t: Check whether R explains the name or only gives the formula.

x: Zinc displaces hydrogen from HCl: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, giving salt and hydrogen gas. Salt and water come from neutralisation.
t: Recall that metals plus acids give salt and hydrogen.
